text: Late at night Suki was frying onions when she heard the back door handle turn, slowly, though she lived alone and had locked it. She froze with the spatula in the air. The oil hissed. Her heart slammed so hard she could feel it in her throat. The handle turned again. She reached, very slowly, for the knife block, her hand trembling, and backed toward the hallway without taking her eyes off the door. Her breath came fast and shallow. Every shadow in the kitchen looked like a shape. She fumbled her phone out of her pocket with fingers that would not work properly.

Hana turned from the stove to find the pan had caught, flames licking up the wall toward the cupboards. For a second she could not move at all. Then smoke rolled across the ceiling and the alarm began to shriek. Her heart hammered. The baby was asleep upstairs. She grabbed a wet towel and threw it over the pan with shaking hands, and the flames leapt around it. Heat scorched her arms. She did not know if she should run for the baby or keep fighting the fire, and the seconds stretched out long and loud, and her legs felt like water.

The train stopped dead in the tunnel and the lights went out. In the pitch dark someone screamed. Esme gripped the pole, her palms slick. There was a smell of burning. Nobody announced anything. Her heart raced and her chest felt tight as a drum; she could not get a full breath. She thought of the stories on the news, the crush of people, the smoke in narrow tunnels. Somewhere a child was sobbing. The minutes went by, and the smell grew stronger, and her whole body was braced, every muscle locked, waiting for whatever was coming.

Driving to work in heavy fog, Bram saw brake lights flare ahead too late. He stamped on the pedal. The car slid, tires screaming, toward the truck in front, and in the mirror he saw headlights rushing up behind him. Time went thick and slow. His hands locked on the wheel and his whole body went rigid; his breath stopped. The car stopped a hand's width from the truck. Then the car behind hit him, and he was thrown forward against the belt. He sat there shaking violently, his heart pounding in his ears, unable to let go of the wheel.

At two in the morning Kai's phone rang with his mother's number. She never called at night. He grabbed it, his heart already racing, and heard only breathing, and then a crash, and then the line went dead. He called back. No answer. He called again. His hands were shaking so badly he could barely press the screen. She lived three hours away, alone. He pulled on his jeans in the dark, missing the leg twice, his mind flooding with pictures of her on the kitchen floor. His mouth was dry as paper and his chest felt tight.

A man called Una's phone saying he was from the police and that her son had been in an accident. He would not say which hospital. He said she needed to stay on the line. Una's legs went weak and she sat down on the stairs. Her son was not answering his phone. Her heart was banging against her ribs, and the room seemed to shrink around her. The voice on the line kept asking for her bank details. Something was wrong with all of it, but she could not think clearly, her thoughts scattering like birds every time she tried.

Working late alone in the office, Esme heard the lift arrive on her floor and the doors open. Nobody got out. Then footsteps began, slow, from the far end of the dark corridor. Security had gone home at nine. The footsteps stopped. Esme sat very still behind her monitor, holding her breath, her skin prickling from her scalp to her ankles. Her heart pounded so loudly she was sure it could be heard. The footsteps started again, closer. She slid off her chair and crouched under the desk, trembling, pressing her hand over her mouth.

On the scaffolding eight floors up, Gus felt the plank shift under his boots. He grabbed the rail, and it moved too. Below him the street was tiny, the cars like toys. His stomach dropped and his legs turned to jelly. He could not make himself let go of the rail to reach the ladder. Sweat ran into his eyes. A gust of wind came, and the whole structure groaned and swayed. Gus pressed himself flat against the wall, his heart hammering, his breath coming in short gasps, and shouted for help in a voice he did not recognize.

Pia was pulling weeds by the shed when she saw the snake coiled under the watering can, its head raised, a hand's length from her fingers. She went completely still. Her heart leapt into her throat and stayed there. She had read that this kind was venomous. Sweat broke out on her upper lip. The snake's tongue flickered. She did not dare breathe. Very, very slowly, she began to draw her hand back, every muscle in her arm trembling with the effort of moving smoothly, her eyes locked on those small dark eyes.

Weeding along the fence at dusk, Lior heard a low growl and looked up to see a large dog, loose, its hackles up, standing at the gate he had left open. It was staring at him. His grandson was playing on the lawn behind him. Lior's heart kicked hard against his ribs. He stood up slowly, putting himself between the dog and the boy, the trowel shaking in his hand. The dog took a step forward and growled again, lips pulled back over its teeth. Lior's mouth went dry, and his legs felt as though they might give way.

The doctor looked at the scan for a long time without saying anything, then called a colleague in. They spoke quietly in the corner. Vera sat on the edge of the bed in the paper gown, her hands gripping the sheet. Her heart was racing. Nobody would meet her eyes. The colleague pointed at something on the screen. Vera's stomach twisted and a cold sweat broke out on her back. She wanted to ask what they had seen and could not make her voice work. The clock on the wall ticked, and every tick seemed to take a very long time.

Waiting for the biopsy results, Femi sat in the clinic corridor jiggling his leg so hard the chair rattled. His hands were cold and clammy. Every time a door opened his head snapped up, and every time it was someone else's name. He kept picturing the word the doctor might say. His heart thudded in his chest and his breath came short. He had not slept for three nights. When a nurse finally came toward him holding a folder, his whole body went rigid, his throat closed, and he found that he could not stand up.

The envelope had no stamp and no return address, and inside was a photograph of Noor's front door, taken at night, and a single line: we know where you live. Noor dropped it on the hall floor. She checked the lock, then checked it again. Her heart was pounding so hard her vision swam. She went from window to window, drawing the curtains, peering out at the dark street, where a car was parked with its engine running. Her hands shook. She crouched by the radiator with her phone, trying to remember the number for the police.

The parcel on Ivo's doorstep was ticking. He heard it as he bent to pick it up and froze, his hand an inch from the brown paper. He was not expecting anything. The ticking went on, steady and loud in the silent street. Ivo backed away, step by step, his heart racing, sweat prickling under his collar. His legs wanted to run and would not. When he reached the gate he turned and ran down the road, his breath rasping in his chest, and did not stop until he was at the corner, where he fumbled for his phone.

Zola's dog had eaten something in the park and now lay on the kitchen floor, shaking and foaming at the mouth. His eyes were rolling. Zola knelt beside him with her hands on his heaving side, her heart hammering. The vet's line was busy. She tried again and again. The dog's breathing was ragged and quick. She could not think; her thoughts kept spinning. She wrapped him in a blanket, carried him to the car, and then could not get the key into the ignition because her hands were trembling so badly.

At night Nell woke to find her cat standing rigid on the end of the bed, fur on end, staring at the bedroom door, growling low in its throat. From the hallway came a creak, then another. Nell lived alone. She lay without moving, her heart pounding so hard it shook her. The cat hissed. Another creak, closer. Her skin went cold and every hair on her arms stood up. She groped for her phone on the bedside table, knocking over a glass, and the sound was huge in the silence, and the creaking stopped.

On the first night in the new flat, Tavi heard someone trying keys in her front door. She had moved in that afternoon. The previous tenant, the landlord had said, had left owing money to some rough people. The scraping went on, one key after another. Tavi stood in the dark hallway with her back pressed against the wall, her heart thudding, holding her breath. She had not even put up the chain. Her mouth was dry. Slowly, trembling, she reached out and slid the chain into place, flinching at the tiny metallic click.

Carrying the last box up the stairs of his new building, Eli stepped onto a landing that cracked and sagged under his weight. He looked down and saw daylight through the gap in the boards, three floors down. He froze. The box was heavy in his arms and the boards groaned. His heart was galloping. He could not go forward or back without shifting his weight. Sweat ran down his spine. Very slowly he let the box slide to the floor, and it crashed through, and he heard it hit the ground far below, and his knees nearly gave out.

Riding downhill fast, Wren squeezed the brakes and felt nothing: the cable had snapped. The bicycle picked up speed. At the bottom of the hill was a busy junction and the lights were red. Her heart jumped into her mouth. The wind roared in her ears and her eyes watered. She dragged her feet on the road, and her shoes burned and bounced. Cars were crossing below. She could not steer onto the grass; there was a wall. Every muscle clenched, her breath locked in her chest, she aimed for the gap between the cars and shut her eyes.

Cycling home on a dark country lane, Amir heard an engine behind him, very close and not slowing. The headlights filled the road around him. He moved as far to the edge as he could, the hedge scratching his arm, and the car stayed right behind him, revving. His heart was hammering and his legs felt weak on the pedals. The driver leaned on the horn. Amir's hands were slick on the handlebars. There was nowhere to go. He could hear laughter from inside the car, and the engine roared, and it came closer.

In the crowded market Hana let go of her daughter's hand for one second to pay, and when she turned back the girl was gone. Hana spun around. Stalls, legs, bags, noise. Her heart gave a sickening lurch. She shouted her daughter's name, and her voice came out high and strange. People stared. She pushed through the crowd, her chest so tight she could hardly breathe, scanning every small figure in a red coat. None of them were her. The world narrowed to a tunnel. Her legs were shaking and her mouth tasted of metal.

A man at the market had been following Rhea from stall to stall for twenty minutes. Whenever she looked back he was there, a few steps behind, not buying anything. Her heart began to thud. She walked faster, and so did he. The market was emptying as it grew dark. She turned down an aisle between the stalls and heard his footsteps turn too. Her skin prickled and a cold feeling crept up her back. She clutched her bag against her chest, her breath coming quick, and looked around for anyone at all who might help.

The storm had knocked out the power, and Cleo sat in the dark living room listening to the wind. Then came a crack like a gunshot, and the old oak outside began to groan. She saw it lean, through the streaming window, toward the roof above the children's bedroom. Her heart leapt. She was up the stairs before she knew it, her legs shaking, her pulse roaring in her ears. The groaning grew louder. She scooped the sleeping children out of their beds, one under each arm, and ran, not knowing if she would be fast enough.

Rain had been falling for three days, and in the afternoon the water began coming under Oren's front door. Within an hour it was up to his ankles, cold and brown, and still rising. The radio said the river had burst its banks upstream. Oren carried his elderly father up the stairs, his heart hammering, his breath short. The water was climbing the steps behind them. From the upstairs window he could see cars floating in the street. His father kept asking what was happening. Oren's hands would not stop shaking as he tried to call for help.

Noor's friend came to visit, and halfway through the meal she began to clutch her throat. Her face swelled and her lips turned a strange color. She had eaten the sauce with nuts in it. Noor's heart lurched. Her friend was gasping, her eyes wide. Where was the pen, the injector, which bag. Noor tore through the handbag, spilling everything, her hands shaking so badly she dropped it twice. Her friend slid off the chair onto the floor. Noor's whole body flooded with cold, and she shouted for her neighbor, her voice cracking.

Late in the evening Quin's friend, visiting from out of town, went out to buy cigarettes and did not come back. An hour passed. Then two. His phone went straight to voicemail. Quin paced the flat, his heart thumping, checking the window again and again. The neighborhood was rough at night, and his friend did not know it. Every siren made Quin's stomach clench. He pictured an alley, a knife. His palms were sweating. At midnight he grabbed his coat and went out into the dark streets, his breath shallow, calling his friend's name.

On the mountain road at night, the headlights of Sami's old car flickered and died. The road ahead vanished into black. On one side, he knew, was a sheer drop. He braked hard, heart hammering, and the car skidded on loose gravel. He could hear stones rattling down the slope below. The car stopped. He sat gripping the wheel in total darkness, his breath loud, sweat running down his face, not daring to move in case the edge was right under his wheels. A truck's horn sounded somewhere above, coming down the bend toward him.

Teo smelled smoke in his old car on the motorway, and then saw it curling out from under the bonnet. He was in the fast lane, with trucks on both sides. His heart began to pound. He flicked on the hazard lights with a shaking hand and tried to move across, but nobody let him in. The smoke thickened and he could see a flicker of orange at the edge of the bonnet. His chest tightened until he could hardly breathe. He wrenched the wheel and forced his way across the lanes, horns blaring, his whole body rigid.

Bea arrived at the school gate and her son was not there. The teacher said he had left with a man who said he was his uncle. Bea's son did not have an uncle. The ground seemed to drop away beneath her. Her heart was slamming against her ribs, her hands icy. She heard herself asking, in a thin high voice, what the man looked like, which way they went. Her legs were shaking. Other parents were gathering around. She could not breathe properly, could not think, could only see the empty space where her son should be.

Waiting at the school gate, Rafa saw black smoke pouring from a window at the back of the building. The fire alarm began to wail. Children streamed out across the playground in lines, and he searched every face. His daughter's class came out; she was not with them. Every muscle in his body locked. A teacher was shouting a name. Rafa pushed toward the gate and a firefighter held him back. His heart was pounding so hard he could hear nothing else. He stood pressed against the railings, shaking, staring at the smoke, waiting for any sign of her.

Swimming off the beach, Yara felt the current take hold of her and pull her out, fast. She swam hard for the shore and the shore kept getting farther away. Her arms burned. Water slapped her face and she swallowed some and choked. Her heart was racing and her breath came in ragged gasps. The people on the beach were tiny now. She waved an arm and went under, came up coughing, her legs heavy as stone. A cold certainty spread through her chest that she could not keep this up much longer.

Diving from the rocks into the lake, Zeb came up under the floating dock. He hit his head on the planks and there was no air, only dark water and the underside of the boards. He pushed against them and they did not move. His lungs were burning. He clawed along the slimy wood, searching for the edge, his heart pounding in his skull, bubbles escaping from his mouth. He could not tell which way was out. Every direction was the same greenish dark. His chest was convulsing, and he kicked blindly, arms outstretched, and felt his strength draining away.
